sentences.text: Coloborhynchus is a genus of pterodactyloid pterosaur classified within the family Anhangueridae.
The genus name Coloborhynchus means "maimed beak," referring to the damaged and eroded condition of the original fossil.
The specific name clavirostris means "key snout," referring to the shape of the snout in cross-section.
The final two preserved pairs of teeth in Coloborhynchus pointed downward.
The rosette at the tip of the Coloborhynchus snout was robust and box-shaped, unlike the rounded and spoon-shaped rosettes of related Anhanguera species.
The front margin of the Coloborhynchus snout was straight and began at the tip, unlike the curved margins that start further back in related species.
The genus Coloborhynchus was named by Richard Owen in 1874.
Richard Owen named the species Coloborhynchus clavirostris in 1874 based on a partial snout fossil found in the Hastings beds of the Wealden Group in East Sussex, England.
The genus was revived in 1994 when Yuong-Nam Lee named C. wadleighi based on a snout found in 1992 in the Paw Paw Formation of Texas.

A second specimen of Coloborhynchus showing unique features was reported to Alexander Kellner by Darren Naish in 2007, likely representing a second specimen of C. clavirostris that remains undescribed.
Some studies have recovered Coloborhynchus as a member of the family Ornithocheiridae.
Many analyses from 2019 and 2020 recovered Coloborhynchus within the family Anhangueridae, specifically in the subfamily Coloborhynchinae.
The parent group of Coloborhynchus is Coloborhynchinae.
Coloborhynchus belongs to the family Anhangueridae.
C. clavirostris, named by Owen in 1874, is the type species of the genus.
According to a 2008 re-evaluation, Coloborhynchus clavirostris can only be differentiated from relatives based on a unique combination of tooth socket positions.
Coloborhynchus fossils have been found in the Lower Cretaceous of England, dating from 140 to 136 million years ago.
Coloborhynchus lived from the Berriasian to the Cenomanian, between 139.1 and 93.9 million years ago.
Depending on which species are included, Coloborhynchus may also have lived during the Albian and Cenomanian ages, between 113 and 93.9 million years ago.
Reginald Walter Hooley argued that the defining jaw trait was an artifact of erosion and that Coloborhynchus was indistinguishable from Criorhynchus simus.
In 1913, Reginald Walter Hooley concluded that the high tooth position was an erosion effect and that the genus was indistinguishable from Criorhynchus simus.
In 1967, Kuhn agreed with Hooley that Coloborhynchus clavirostris was a synonym of Criorhynchus simus.
Rodrigues and Kellner disagreed with this classification, noting that both lacked the straight crest starting at the snout tip or teeth pointing to the sides as seen in C. clavirostris.
A 2023 review suggested that the traits distinguishing Nicorhynchus from Coloborhynchus were subtle enough to justify synonymizing the two genera.

Kellner, who considered Uktenadactylus a distinct genus in 2008, also considered Siroccopteryx different, noting it lacked the unique dental row characteristics of Coloborhynchus, a view supported by Fastnacht in 2001.
According to Kellner, C. capito is too incomplete for a full comparison with C. clavirostris, and its precise classification remains open to debate.

He noted that C. sedgwickii lacks the unique characteristics of C. clavirostris (in fact, it completely lacks a crest) and may even belong to the same genus as "Ornithocheirus" compressirostris (=Lonchodectes).
